blurb: Grippers, hands, and process tools — parallel-jaw to vacuum, soft, jamming, and dexterous — compared on task fit, versatility, reliability, and cost.
question: How should this robot grasp and work?
title: Robot End Effectors: A Practical Reference
lede: The end effector is where a robot's capital finally touches its work, and it is chosen backwards: from the object and the task, not from the robot. This guide catalogs {{N_ENTRIES}} effector types across six classes — grippers, suction, soft and dexterous hands, and the process tools that do the actual work of industry.

parts.name: Suction & Field
parts.blurb: vacuum and magnets — grab by surface, not shape

parts.name: Soft & Compliant
parts.blurb: gentle grasping of fragile, irregular objects

parts.blurb: tool changers and sensing behind the gripper

facets.label: Task fit
facets.tip: Task families where the effector is a natural first choice — directional, and most cells mix effectors.

facets.label: Versatility
facets.tip: How wide a range of objects and tasks one unit handles without retooling: Single-task (engineered per part) · Moderate (a part family) · Broad (most objects in a category) · Near-universal (the anything-goes aspiration).

facets.label: Reliability
facets.tip: Field-proven robustness at industrial duty cycles: Industrial-proven = decades of 24/7 fleet data · Good = solid with maintenance · Mixed = works but with known operational headaches · Fragile = handle with engineering care.

facets.label: Maturity
facets.tip: Ubiquitous = standard equipment across industry · Common = established in its niche · Emerging = shipping but young · Research = lab stage.

facets.label: Cost
facets.tip: Directional unit cost for a robot-ready effector, excluding the robot and cell engineering around it.
